summary:
GreenSpace tells a farmer the one change that keeps their crop year working as the climate shifts. It splits the year into growth stages, from sowing to harvest, and checks every stage against heat, warm nights, rainfall and soil health using NASA POWER, MODIS, SMAP and GPM data. It then ranks the smallest fixes, such as sowing a week earlier, with the effect, soil impact and confidence of each.

Farmers see their field three ways: past seasons, this season, and the 2040s. Past data alone cannot predict next season, and climate models alone diverge, so GreenSpace combines both with live local observations.

We tested it against history. Using only data from October 2021, it flagged wheat grain filling and advised sowing on 28 October instead of 5 November, cutting grain-fill heat by 43%. Months later, March 2022 became the hottest March in 122 years.

The approach is built to extend to other crops and regions. We proved it first on the rice-wheat year in Punjab, India. GreenSpace can't tell you what next season will do. No tool honestly can. What it shows is how the odds are shifting and the one change that tips them back in your favour, while the final call stays with the farmer and local expertise.

The problem 
In Punjab, India, rice and wheat share one field each year. The day rice leaves the field sets the day wheat is sown, and that decides how much of wheat grain filling falls in the March heat. Warming does not break this year all at once. It breaks single stages more and more often. Farmers need to know which stage is weakening and what the cheapest fix is. 

What GreenSpace does 
GreenSpace keeps the rotation farmers already trust and checks it stage by stage. It then suggests the smallest change that keeps the year working, with its trade-off shown. 

How it works:  

  1. Stage. The farmer's planting dates set 15 growth stages (7 rice, 8 wheat). Ten are checked by 24 rules for heat, warm nights, rain, sunshine and crop pace. Each rule names its source: the Punjab Agricultural University Package of Practices, IRRI, IMD, Lobell et al. 2012 (34 °C for wheat grain filling) or Jagadish et al. 2007 (35 °C for rice flowering). 
  2. Compare. A season counts as bad when it is worse than 8 in 10 normal seasons. We count bad seasons in three views: the 1991-2020 normal and the last ten seasons from NASA POWER, and five NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models for 2021-2040. 
  3. Vote. Three checks act as voters: are recent seasons worse, is there a real trend, do the models show it getting worse? Three votes give high confidence, two give medium, and fewer keep the usual plan. 
  4. Fix. The engine tries the cheapest change first (timing, method, variety, adding a crop, swapping a crop) and re-checks the whole year, so side effects show up. 

 

 

Result for Ludhiana 

Bad grain-fill heat happens in 2 seasons in 10 in the normal, 3 in 10 lately and 4 in 10 in the climate models. Sowing wheat on 28 October instead of 5 November brings it to 1 in 10. The trade-off, shown in the app, is that warm nights early in the wheat season rise from 1 to 8 in 10. 

Proof: the 2022 heatwave 

 

We planned the 2021-22 season as the engine would have on 15 October 2021, then replayed the real season on NASA POWER. Seen from 2021, grain filling showed early warnings, not a red flag. The heatwave then broke both grain-fill limits, on NASA POWER and at the NOAA station in Patiala. Sowing on 28 October would have cut grain-fill heat by 43% (19 days above 34 °C instead of 22) and freed the field by 4 April for summer moong. Over many held-out seasons, flagged seasons broke their limit 22% of the time against 9% for unflagged ones. GreenSpace spots rising risk; it does not predict the year. 

What the farmer sees 
A map to pick the field, a card per stage (OK, Watch or Change), a circular Year Dial with a draggable planting date, the suggested change with before and after odds, a "Why this?" card with sources, soil, water and nutrient cards, 25 years of NASA POWER history, and labels in English, Punjabi and Hindi. 

Why it is different 
Most tools give one score per season or say which crop to grow next. GreenSpace checks both crops and the handover between them, merges past, present and future into one count with a confidence label, and shows the trade-off of every fix. The method extends to other districts, crops and rotations. 

Built with 
Python (pandas, numpy, FastAPI); React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, deck.gl with H3 hexagons, React Three Fiber; deployed on Render. 

Honest limits 
One district and one rotation today. NASA POWER cells are about 50 km wide, so values are regional. Soil comes from SoilGrids at district scale. Stage lengths, the 8-in-10 line and the voting scheme are our design choices, labelled as such.
